questions.prompt: Complete the cost-optimization table. Type the optimization lever or inference mode that most directly fits each workload symptom.

need.template: A large, stable instruction/reference prefix repeats across many requests.
Conversation history grows until every turn sends lots of stale context.
Simple classification traffic is routed to the most expensive high-capability model.
Sustained predictable Bedrock demand justifies reserved model capacity.

questions.explanation: Prompt caching helps when a supported stable prefix is reused; context pruning/summarization removes low-value repeated history; model routing/cascading avoids paying for excess capability on simple requests; and Provisioned Throughput fits sustained predictable demand where reserved capacity is justified. Each lever targets a different cost driver, so applying all of them blindly can add complexity without benefit.
hints: Identify what is being wasted: repeated prefix tokens, stale history, excessive model capability, or capacity shape.

questions.prompt: Users report slow time-to-first-token. A trace shows: retrieval 1.8 s, model first token 0.35 s, tool calls 0.1 s. Diagnose and optimize the measured bottleneck.

steps.prompt: Which stage is the primary measured bottleneck?

choices.label: Browser rendering, even though it is not in the provided trace

steps.prompt: What should the team investigate first in that stage?

choices.label: Vector-store/query latency, filters/top-k, reranking, network path, and index/query design
Immediately replace the FM without profiling retrieval

steps.prompt: The trace shows expensive reranking over far too many candidates, with no quality gain beyond the top subset. What is the targeted change?

choices.label: Reduce candidate/top-k/reranking work to the evaluated level that preserves required retrieval quality
Buy Provisioned Throughput even though the measured model stage is already 0.35 s
Re-run representative load/evaluation and confirm retrieval + end-to-end latency improve without unacceptable retrieval/answer-quality regression

questions.explanation: The trace already localizes the dominant delay to retrieval, so changing the model first is not evidence-based. Profile the slow stage, then change the specific expensive operation—in this case excess candidate/reranking work—at a level proven to preserve retrieval quality. Verification must check a representative latency distribution and quality together; optimizing p50 or one query can hide tail regressions, and reducing retrieval work too far can harm grounded answers.
hints: Use the measured stage timings before choosing an optimization.

questions.prompt: Build a useful GenAI observability model. Assign the signal family that best answers each operational question.

slots.label: Are APIs/model calls healthy, fast, and within quota?
Which model/prompt version, token usage, and stop/safety outcomes produced this result?
Which retrieved chunks/tool calls/agent steps contributed and where was time spent?
Did the application complete the user/business task with acceptable quality?
Can we reconstruct who changed/invoked governed AWS resources and correlate the execution later?

questions.explanation: GenAI observability has to connect infrastructure health to model behavior, retrieval/agent execution, user/business quality, and audit evidence. A dashboard with only uptime and CPU cannot explain a groundedness regression, a bad tool decision, or which prompt/model version produced an incident. The useful design is correlated across these layers with trace/request identifiers.
hints: Each slot asks a different question; choose the signal family that can actually answer it.
